newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada gets tough on tobacco.
newsitem.headline: Canada gets tough on tobacco.

text.p: Canada's powerful tobacco industry is reeling from a triple-barrelled assault by the federal government, local authorities and a potentially costly lawsuit.

The Canadian government recently proposed legislation to ban most tobacco advertising, restrict tobacco sponsorship of cultural and sports events and give the government sweeping powers to regulate the contents of cigarettes. The measure, which has gathered support from all parties in Parliament, is likely to pass next year.
In addition, several Canadian cities, including the country's most populous -- Toronto -- have passed measures to ban smoking in restaurants and bars.
Meanwhile, a lawsuit by four Toronto residents threatens large damages against tobacco manufacturers.
"Trashing the tobacco industry has become a national sport," said Marie-Josee Lapointe, spokeswoman for the Canadian Tobacco Manufacturers' Council, a lobbying group.
Canada's tobacco industry contends the federal legislation, which has been hailed by most health groups, goes too far and says it plans a court challenge.
The anti-tobacco bill is "extreme, ineffective and quite possibly illegal," Lapointe said.

The industry lobbied hard to stall the introduction of the bill, and Health Minister David Dingwall said he was warned that tobacco companies planned similar tactics to delay its passage through Parliament.
Canada's tobacco industry is about 65 percent controlled by Imperial Tobacco Ltd., a unit of Imasco Ltd. Imasco is 40 percent owned by Britain's B.A.T. Industries Plc.
Another big Canadian cigarette company is Rothmans, Benson and Hedges Inc., 60 percent-owned by Rothmans Inc. -- a unit of Rothmans International Plc -- and 40 percent by Philip Morris Cos. Inc.
A third major player is RJR MacDonald, wholly owned by RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. unit R.J. Reynolds Tobacco International.
LOCAL GOVERNMENTS AGAINST TOBACCO
Local governments across Canada are also lining up against tobacco.

In July, Toronto passed a law that effectively bans smoking in the city's restaurants and bars. The controversial measure, which takes effect in January, was described as the toughest in North America.
Similar bans were also approved in Vancouver and Ottawa.
Toronto City Councilor Peter Tabuns said the law was driven by many councilors' personal experiences.
"A lot of the councilors have had exposure in the form of friends and family dying of one form of cancer or another," Tabuns said.
Roberta Ferrence, a University of Toronto health advocate, said personal experiences played a big part in hardening Canadians' attitudes toward smoking.
"There has been a gradual change in people's mindsets over the past 30 years as the true effects of smoking have become known and people are being confronted with the realities of the habit."

About 36,325 deaths across Canada were indirectly attributed to smoking in 1991, the last year for which such an estimate was available. It is estimated that about 48 billion cigarettes were smoked in 1993 in Canada, a country of about 30 million people.
CANADIANS CHALLENGE TOBACCO IN COURT

Such statistics prompted four Toronto residents to sue the tobacco industry. They hope to turn the case into a class-action lawsuit that might compel tobacco companies to compensate all Canadians using their product.
The four are each suing the tobacco industry for C$1 million ($730,000) in hopes of reclaiming money spent on cigarettes to compensate for the "loss of quality of life."

If an Ontario judge agrees with the plaintiffs' contention that the lawsuit should be a class action, the tobacco industry could face paying billions of dollars in damages to Canada's estimated 7 million smokers.
The lawsuit is the first of its kind in Canada. A number of U.S. states have sued the industry in hopes of recovering government money spent on smoking-related illnesses.
CANADA LOOKING SOUTH FOR CLUES IN TOBACCO WAR
It is not the first time Canada has followed the U.S. lead in tackling the tobacco industry.

The decision by the Canadian government to try to regulate the contents of cigarettes came after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced plans to regulate cigarettes as a "drug delivery device."

Luc Marpial, spokesman for the Canadian Council on Smoking and Health, said although Canadians' attitudes toward smoking were generally more negative than those of Americans, it was normal for Canada to wait for Washington before introducing legislation.
"A lot of what's happening in the U.S. is prompting Canada to move forward. It would seem sometimes that we need an extra push," he said.
Canadian attitudes toward smoking and the tobacco industry have hardened.

Despite the new anti-tobacco measures, a national poll taken by the Angus Reid Group earlier this year showed that 32 percent of Canadians think smoking restrictions "have not gone far enough" to protect public health.
